newsitem.title: THAILAND: Long-awaited Thai censure debate begins.
newsitem.headline: Long-awaited Thai censure debate begins.

text.p: The long-awaited no-confidence debate against Thai prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa began on Wednesday with the leader of the six-party coalition government expected to face tough attacks by the opposition.

Banharn said on Tuesday he was confident that he would fare well in the debate. The motion tabled by the opposition accuses him of incompetence and economic mismanagement, among other things. He has denied the charges.

Banharn's coalition controls 209 of the 391 seats in parliament. Political analysts believe that, for the moment, Banharn's coalition partners will support him and he is expected to win when the vote comes.

"This is the toughest time for him because he is the sole target of the attack," Kanchana Silpa-archa, Banharn's daughter and a member of parliament for his Chart Thai party, told reporters. "I have asked him to retire from politics and will continue to try and pursuade him."
Banharn's 14-month old government has been under sharp criticism from the opposition and local media over its handling of the economy and domestic politics.
Speculation was rife in the run-up to the debate that Banharn might resign and hand the premiership to a more acceptable politician or even dissolve parliament before the debate.
But Banharn vowed to fight the accusations in parliament.
The televised debate is expected to last for three days, the government whip said on Wednesday.

About 7,000 people, mostly from Banharn's home province of Suphan Buri and other Chart Thai stronghold provinces in central Thailand, were camped out in a plaza near the parliament. The well-organised supporters, who arrived in more than 100 busses early on Wednesday, came to cheer on Banharn.
"We came to lend moral support to the prime minister and back him to fight for our nation," Vijit Radnai of Suphan Buri told Reuters.
Hundreds of anti-riot and plainclothes police were deployed near the parliament in anticipation of large groups who were expected to show up later.
